messages.content: Write the introduction to a monthly engineering newsletter whose theme this month is technical debt. Around 200 words.

output:
Here's the draft. Bracketed bits are placeholders for your real names/details.

---

Nobody schedules technical debt. It accumulates the way silt does — one deadline at a time, each of them reasonable at the time.

That's the honest version. The dishonest version is the one where we all agree the debt was a mistake, promise to pay it down next quarter, and then ship the next thing instead. We've done that. Twice, at least.

So this month isn't a cleanup sprint. It's an inventory. Three teams went back through the parts of the codebase they dread touching and wrote down why — not "it's messy," but what specifically breaks, how long a change takes, who gets paged when it doesn't work. [Name]'s piece on the auth service is the sharpest thing I've read internally this year, and the root cause turns out to be a [2019] decision nobody here can still explain.

You'll also find a short defense of leaving debt alone. Some of it is load-bearing. Some of it lives in code we're deleting in eight months anyway, and rewriting that now is just a costlier way to delete it.

Read the inventory. Argue with it. That's the point.

---

~205 words. Two things worth knowing about the choices: the opening rejects the usual "debt is a metaphor from finance" framing, which every debt newsletter opens with, and the closing avoids a moral so the pieces themselves carry the argument. If your culture is more formal than this reads, tell me and I'll pull the register up a notch without flattening the cadence.
